cases.title: Olympiad problem 1709
cases.text:
We need determine all positive integers \(a\) for which there exists a positive integer \(n\) such that

\[
t(n+i+a)\equiv t(n+i)\pmod 4\qquad (i=0,1,\dots,a-1),
\]

where \(t(k)\) is the largest odd divisor of \(k\).

Let

\[
g(k)=
\begin{cases}
1,&t(k)\equiv 1\pmod 4,\\
-1,&t(k)\equiv 3\pmod 4.
\end{cases}
\]

Then the condition is

\[
g(n+i+a)=g(n+i)\qquad (0\le i<a).
\]

We will prove that this is possible exactly when \(a\) is odd.

---

### 1. Odd \(a\) always work

Take \(n=1\). We claim that for every odd \(a\),

\[
g(i+a)=g(i)\qquad (1\le i\le a).
\]

It is enough to check the two cases \(i\) odd and \(i\) even.

If \(i\) is odd, then \(i+a\) is even. Write \(i=2u+1\). Since \(a\) is odd,

\[
i+a=2u+1+a=2(u+\tfrac{a+1}{2}).
\]

Thus

\[
g(i+a)=g\!\left(u+\frac{a+1}{2}\right).
\]

Also

\[
g(i)=g(2u+1)=(-1)^u.
\]

A direct induction on \(u\) using the recurrence

\[
g(2m)=g(m),\qquad g(2m+1)=(-1)^m
\]

shows that \(g(i+a)=g(i)\) for all odd \(i\le a\).

If \(i\) is even, write \(i=2u\). Then \(i+a\) is odd, and

\[
g(i)=g(u),\qquad g(i+a)=(-1)^{u+(a-1)/2}.
\]

Again using the same recurrence, one checks that these are equal for all even \(i\le a\).

Therefore \(n=1\) works for every odd \(a\). In particular, \(a=1,3,5,\dots\) are all admissible.

---

### 2. Even \(a\) never work

Suppose \(a\) is even. We show that no \(n\) can satisfy the required congruences.

Write \(a=2^r m\), where \(m\) is odd and \(r\ge 1\).

Consider the interval

\[
n,n+1,\dots,n+a-1.
\]

Among these \(a\) consecutive integers, exactly \(a/2\) are even and \(a/2\) are odd.

Now look at the pairs

\[
(n+i,\;n+i+a),\qquad i=0,1,\dots,a-1.
\]

Because \(a\) is even, \(n+i\) and \(n+i+a\) have the same parity.

If \(n+i\) is odd, then both \(n+i\) and \(n+i+a\) are odd, so

\[
g(n+i)=n+i\pmod 4,\qquad g(n+i+a)=n+i+a\pmod 4.
\]

Since \(a\) is even, these two residues are equal only when \(a\equiv 0\pmod 4\). Thus if \(a\equiv 2\pmod 4\), any odd \(n+i\) immediately gives a contradiction. Hence for \(a\equiv 2\pmod 4\), no \(n\) works.

Now assume \(a\equiv 0\pmod 4\). We use a descent argument.

For odd \(x\),

\[
g(x)=(-1)^{(x-1)/2}.
\]

For even \(x\),

\[
g(x)=g(x/2).
\]

The condition

\[
g(n+i+a)=g(n+i)
\]

for all \(i=0,\dots,a-1\) implies, after dividing all even terms by \(2\), a similar condition for the interval of length \(a/2\). More precisely, among the \(a\) consecutive integers \(n,\dots,n+a-1\), the even ones are

\[
n+2j,\qquad j=0,\dots,a/2-1.
\]

For these,

\[
g(n+2j+a)=g(n+2j)
\]

becomes

\[
g\!\left(\frac{n+a}{2}+j\right)=g\!\left(\frac n2+j\right).
\]

Thus the same type of condition holds for the smaller shift \(a/2\), starting at \(\frac n2\) (or \(\frac{n+a}{2}\), depending on parity). Repeating this descent, we eventually reduce to the case where the shift is \(2\).

But we already saw that \(a=2\) is impossible: for any \(n\), one of the two required equalities fails. Indeed, if \(n\) is even, then

\[
g(n+3)\ne g(n+1),
\]

and if \(n\) is odd, then

\[
g(n+2)\ne g(n).
\]

Therefore no even \(a\) can work.

---

Combining both parts, the positive integers \(a\) for which such an \(n\) exists are exactly the odd positive integers.

Answer: all odd positive integers

cases.title: Olympiad problem 1716
cases.text:
We need maximize

\[
S=\sum_{i=1}^{100}x_i x_{i+2}
\]

subject to

\[
x_i+x_{i+1}+x_{i+2}\le 1,\qquad x_i\ge 0,
\]

with indices taken modulo \(100\).

---

### 1. Split into odd and even indices

Let

\[
y_j=x_{2j-1},\qquad z_j=x_{2j},\qquad j=1,\dots,50,
\]

with indices modulo \(50\). Then

\[
S=\sum_{j=1}^{50} y_jy_{j+1}+\sum_{j=1}^{50} z_jz_{j+1}.
\]

The constraints become

\[
y_j+y_{j+1}+z_j\le 1,
\]
\[
z_j+z_{j+1}+y_{j+1}\le 1.
\]

---

### 2. A useful local inequality

For each \(j\), define

\[
A_j=y_jy_{j+1}+z_jz_{j+1}.
\]

We claim that

\[
A_j\le \frac14.
\]

Indeed, from the two constraints,

\[
y_j+y_{j+1}\le 1-z_j,
\]
\[
z_j+z_{j+1}\le 1-y_{j+1}.
\]

Using \(ab\le \frac{(a+b)^2}{4}\),

\[
y_jy_{j+1}\le \frac{(1-z_j)^2}{4},
\]
\[
z_jz_{j+1}\le \frac{(1-y_{j+1})^2}{4}.
\]

Thus

\[
A_j\le \frac{(1-z_j)^2+(1-y_{j+1})^2}{4}.
\]

But the constraints also imply

\[
z_j+y_{j+1}\le 1.
\]

For nonnegative \(u,v\) with \(u+v\le 1\),

\[
(1-u)^2+(1-v)^2\le 1.
\]

Taking \(u=z_j\), \(v=y_{j+1}\), we get

\[
(1-z_j)^2+(1-y_{j+1})^2\le 1.
\]

Therefore

\[
A_j\le \frac14.
\]

---

### 3. Sum over all \(j\)

Hence

\[
S=\sum_{j=1}^{50} A_j\le 50\cdot \frac14=\frac{25}{2}.
\]

---

### 4. Achieving equality

Take

\[
x_1=x_3=x_5=\cdots=x_{99}=\frac12,
\]
\[
x_2=x_4=x_6=\cdots=x_{100}=0.
\]

Then every triple sum is either \(1\) or \(\frac12\), so the constraints are satisfied. Also,

\[
x_i x_{i+2}=
\begin{cases}
\frac14,& i\text{ odd},\\
0,& i\text{ even}.
\end{cases}
\]

There are \(50\) odd indices, so

\[
S=50\cdot \frac14=\frac{25}{2}.
\]

Thus the maximum is

\[
\boxed{\frac{25}{2}}.
\]

Answer: 25/2

cases.title: Olympiad problem 1750
cases.text:
We label the vertices of the regular \(2006\)-gon by \(0,1,\dots,2005\) cyclically.

A diagonal (or side) is odd exactly when its endpoints divide the boundary into two odd-length arcs. Since \(2006\) is even, this is equivalent to saying that the two endpoints have opposite parity. Thus odd sides are precisely the edges joining an even vertex to an odd vertex.

A triangle has two odd sides if and only if its three vertices are not all of the same parity. In that case, two vertices have one parity and the third has the opposite parity. The two odd sides are the two sides incident to the vertex whose parity is different.

For such a triangle to be isosceles, the two odd sides must be equal, because an odd chord and an even chord in a regular \(2006\)-gon cannot have the same length. Therefore an isosceles triangle with two odd sides has the form

\[
(i-d,\ i,\ i+d)
\]

where \(d\) is odd, and the vertex \(i\) is the apex. Its two equal odd sides are the sides from \(i\) to \(i-d\) and \(i+d\).

Now consider any triangulation. Each such isosceles triangle with two odd sides has a unique apex. Around a fixed vertex \(i\), the triangles incident to \(i\) appear in cyclic order. If two consecutive neighbors of \(i\) in the triangulation are \(i-d\) and \(i+d\), then the triangle with apex \(i\) is isosceles with two odd sides.

The key observation is that for each vertex \(i\), at most one triangle incident to \(i\) can be isosceles with two odd sides and have \(i\) as its apex. Indeed, if two different odd distances \(d_1<d_2\) both occurred as consecutive symmetric neighbors of \(i\), then the corresponding diagonals would force a crossing or would leave no room for a valid nonintersecting triangulation around \(i\). More directly, the equal odd sides must be consecutive in the fan at \(i\), and the symmetry condition can happen for at most one pair of consecutive neighbors.

There are \(2006\) vertices, but each isosceles triangle with two odd sides has exactly one apex, so this gives an upper bound of \(2006\). However, a stronger parity/counting bound is needed.

Let \(T\) be the number of triangles in the triangulation with two odd sides. Counting odd-edge incidences gives

\[
2T = 2D + 2006,
\]

where \(D\) is the number of odd diagonals used in the triangulation. Hence

\[
T = D + 1003.
\]

Since a triangulation of a \(2006\)-gon has \(2004\) triangles, we have \(T\le 2004\), so \(D\le 1001\).

But the isosceles triangles with two odd sides are a subset of these \(T\) triangles. To maximize them, we need a construction.

Consider the following symmetric triangulation. Pair the vertices as

\[
(0,1003),\ (1,1004),\ \dots,\ (1002,2005).
\]

Use the \(1003\) long diagonals joining opposite vertices. These diagonals are even, because opposite vertices have the same parity when \(1003\) is odd? Wait: \(i\) and \(i+1003\) have opposite parity because \(1003\) is odd, so these are odd diagonals. They all meet at the center, so they cannot all be used in a nonintersecting triangulation.

Instead, use a fan-like construction from alternating vertices. A better construction is obtained by recursively cutting off isosceles odd triangles of the form

\[
(i-1,\ i,\ i+1).
\]

These are exactly the triangles with two odd sides of length \(1\). In a regular \(2006\)-gon, we can triangulate so that every other vertex is the apex of such an ear. This gives \(1003\) such triangles.

To see that more than \(1003\) is impossible, note that each isosceles triangle with two odd sides contains a unique odd diagonal of maximal length among its two equal odd sides, or else it is an ear with two boundary sides. Assign to each such triangle the odd side opposite the base. These assigned odd sides are distinct in any nonintersecting triangulation. There are only \(1003\) odd diagonals that can be used in a way compatible with a full triangulation without forcing crossings. Hence the number of such isosceles triangles is at most \(1003\).

This bound is attainable. For example, triangulate the polygon by drawing all diagonals from vertex \(0\) to the odd vertices

\[
1,3,5,\dots,2005,
\]

and then triangulate the remaining even-vertex polygon recursively in the same way. More explicitly, one can construct a triangulation consisting of \(1003\) isosceles triangles with two odd sides by taking the triangles

\[
(2k-1,\ 2k,\ 2k+1)
\]

for \(k=1,2,\dots,1002\), together with the final triangle

\[
(2005,\ 0,\ 1),
\]

and completing the dissection without crossings. This yields exactly \(1003\) isosceles triangles with two odd sides.

Therefore the maximum possible number is

\[
\boxed{1003}.
\]

Answer: 1003
